label: text
text: THE JOLLY CROWDS THAT MADE LONDON GAY.

label: text
text: Although 67 special excursions had been scheduled, many of them had to be run in duplicate to cope with the demand.

label: text
text: The crowds were noisy but good humoured, and railway officials declare that they have never seen a better-behaved invasion.

label: text
text: Fresh crowds arrived every five or ten minutes, many of them singing in chorus. There was a high percentage of women and girls.

label: text
text: The Welsh advance guard reached Padding on at 2 a.m. A huge look was tied to the front of the engine, which was festooned with blue and white streamers.

label: text
text: One party from South Wales had with them four barrels of beer, four gallons of whiskey, four gallons of rum, 22 dozen minerals and 1,500 sandwiches.

label: text
text: Nearly half of this supply was exhausted when their train reached Paddington. "We've had a quiet trip up," said a burly miner, "but we'll be thirsty going back, whatever, and—look you—we shall need to celebrate the victory. Indeed, yes."

label: text
text: A Cup-tie baby girl was born at the Hotel Russell. Her mother, an enthusiastic supporter of Cardiff City, had come all the way from Pontypridd to see the great match at all costs.

label: text
text: Scores of crowded and rather noisy charabancs added to the galley of the London streets: A two-hour tour of London before the match appeared to be included in the programme of many parties.

label: text
text: The men from the North were not quite so strong numerically, but they lacked nothing in enthusiasm. Oldham "did itself proud," and arrived at Euston complete with its own jazz band in carnival dress.

label: text
text: The dour Yorkshiremen had not neglected the commissarlat Organised parties brought their own barrels and crates, and luggage vans had been set aside as beer stores for the travellers.

label: paragraph_title
text: THE AUSSIES.

label: text
text: CAN THEY BE BEATEN?

label: text
text: TEMPERAMENT THE MOST IMPORTANT POINT:

label: text
text: "Temperament is the thing that tells in Test matches. It is not how a man stands in the averages, but how he shapes on big occasions, that should guide the electors of an England eleven." This is the considered opinion of Mr Arthur Gilligan, England's cricket captain, expressed by him to the "Sunday Express."

label: text
text: "Spoforth," added Mr Gilligan, "is reported to have said that he thought the Australians would win in 1926, as he considered they had more nerve. He is right in a way, though I think our fellows put up a pretty stout fight. But the Australians have a wonderful fighting temperament, and I think the most important point for us to study is temperament.

label: text
text: “Never mind how a man stands in the averages—pick him for what he has done on big occasions. Watch him carefully in a difficult match, such as Gentlemen v. Players. You will so often find that a man who does well is smaller matches is finished on a big day. If a match were called Mr. Somebody's team v: Australia instead of England v. Australia, many a cricketer would not feel so overwaved by the importance of the event.

label: text
text: Temperament, though largely a matter of natural character, can be developed to a great degree.

label: text
text: THE LATE TOUR.

label: text
text: Discussing the recent tour, Mr. Gilligan said: "I never noticed any instances of funking by our men; I thought we did remarkably well. But our battling was not so good as that of the Australians. They were good right down to No. II. If we had seven wickets down out last three were more likely to put on ten than a hundred.

label: text
text: "Our bowling was quite as good as theirs, and our fielding definitely superior—as the Australians themselves admitted. I, as a bowler, do not like the eight-ball over. Batsmen don't object to it; for instance, Jack Hobbs is all in favour of it, while Tate is dead against it. Australia is really a batsman's paradise, and the eight-ball over makes life hard for the bowler. The bowler should, in my opinion, be helped, not hindered."

label: text
text: It the summer of 1920 is dry, we shall have a hard struggle with the Australians. Should it be a damp one, England stands a very good chance. The Australians, it will be remembered, made a poor show in the fourth Test match during our recent tour, when the wicket was wet; but on a dry wicket they take full marks.

label: paragraph_title
text: THE DIAGNOSIS.

label: text
text: CRICKET STORY.

label: text
text: For a moment on first waking I was conscious only of a vague discomfort. Something was wrong, but it was not until I attempted to move that I realised how ill I was, writes T. Hodgkinson.

label: text
text: Then however, the ache apparent in every limb and the fact that even breathing was a process not unfraught with pain made it clear that the malady was no triding one. And I confided the fact to Phyllis without delay.

label: text
text: Who wants his breakfast in bed? she asked heartlessly, misled by the brave smile I had assumed.

label: text
text: "Not me," I replied, and noting how illness had weakened my grammar as well as destroyed my appetite, she, too, began to grow concerned.

label: text
text:
"Aching all over," she said
"Sounds like flu. I'd better take your temperature."

label: text
text: Ever since I bit the end off a perfectly new thermometer and for days, owing to the amount of glass I had swallowed, left her, in doubt as to whether to order red or black for her spring costume Phyllis only takes my temperature in extreme cases. That, presumably, was the real reason for her indignation when she discovered that I was quite normal.

label: text
text: You're as well as I am," she declared. "You'll feel much better once you're up."

label: text
text: “I shall have to feel much better before I'm up,” I told her. “I think we ought to have other advice. Haven't you got another thermometer?”

label: text
text: She hadn't, and so great was her faith in the old one that it was only with the greatest difficulty that I persuaded her to send for the doctor.

label: text
text: Tell me the truth," I begged him. "I can bear anything better than suspense." And thus implored, he did so.

label: text
text: "You ought to know better," he said, severely, "than to send for me just because you're a little stiff after your first cricket practice."

text: The committee of the M.C.C. have addressed to the respective Boards of Control of England and Australia and the South African Cricket Association a request that, in order to qualify somewhat the elements of chance in Test matches, they will consider the possibility of making some change in the principle of tossing for innings.
